title: Frequent Itemset Mining
text:
Frequent Itemset Mining (FIM) is a foundational data mining technique used to discover items that frequently co-occur in large transactional datasets. The most classic application is Market Basket Analysis — finding out which products customers tend to buy together (e.g., bread and butter, or diapers and beer).
Beyond retail, FIM powers:

Recommendation Engines: “Customers who bought X also bought Y.”
Bioinformatics: Identifying co-occurring gene mutations.
Web Usage Mining: Discovering pages frequently visited together in a single session.
Healthcare: Finding combinations of symptoms or medications associated with specific outcomes.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining
text:
Core Concepts & Metrics
To evaluate whether an itemset (a collection of one or more items) is “frequent” or interesting, data scientists rely on three primary metrics: Support, Confidence, and Lift.
Suppose one has a dataset of \(N\) total transactions, and is evaluating two itemsets: \(X\) (the antecedent) and \(Y\) (the consequent).

1. Support
Support measures how frequently an itemset appears in the entire dataset. It helps filter out rare, statistically insignificant combinations.
\[\text{Support}(X) = \frac{\text{Transactions containing } X}{N}\]
\[\text{Support}(X \cup Y) = \frac{\text{Transactions containing both } X \text{ and } Y}{N}\]


2. Confidence
Confidence measures the reliability of an association rule (\(X \rightarrow Y\)). It represents the conditional probability that a transaction contains \(Y\), given that it already contains \(X\).
\[\text{Confidence}(X \rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{Support}(X \cup Y)}{\text{Support}(X)}\]


3. Lift
Lift evaluates how much more likely \(Y\) is to be bought when \(X\) is bought, compared to \(Y\)’s baseline popularity. Because high-frequency items (like milk or bananas) naturally appear in many baskets, Confidence alone can be misleading. Lift corrects for this.
\[\text{Lift}(X \rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{Confidence}(X \rightarrow Y)}{\text{Support}(Y)} = \frac{\text{Support}(X \cup Y)}{\text{Support}(X) \times \text{Support}(Y)}\]



Table 1: Interpreting Lift Values









Lift Value
Interpretation




\(\text{Lift} > 1\)
Positive correlation: \(X\) and \(Y\) appear together more often than expected by chance.


\(\text{Lift} = 1\)
Independence: \(X\) and \(Y\) have no relationship; co-occurrence is purely coincidental.


\(\text{Lift} < 1\)
Negative correlation: \(X\) and \(Y\) are substitutes; buying one makes buying the other less likely.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining
text:
How the Algorithms Work
Scanning every possible combination of items in a store with 10,000 products requires checking \(2^{10,000} - 1\) itemsets — a computational impossibility. Two primary algorithms solve this efficiently:

The Apriori Algorithm
Apriori relies on the Downward Closure Property (the Apriori Principle): If an itemset is frequent, all of its subsets must also be frequent. Conversely, if {Milk} is infrequent, {Milk, Cereal} cannot possibly be frequent, allowing the algorithm to prune massive branches of the search tree early.

Pros: Easy to understand and implement.
Cons: Requires multiple scans of the database and generates a large number of candidate itemsets, making it slow on massive datasets.



FP-Growth (Frequent Pattern Growth)
FP-Growth eliminates candidate generation entirely. It scans the dataset twice to compress transactions into a specialized tree structure called an FP-Tree, then recursively mines frequent patterns directly from the tree.

Pros: Significantly faster and more memory-efficient than Apriori on large datasets.
Cons: The FP-Tree can become complex if transactions share very few items.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining
text:
Tutorial
pandas and mlxtend (Machine Learning Extensions) are used to mine frequent itemsets and generate association rules from a simulated grocery dataset.

Step 1: Environment Setup
Install mlxtend, if it is not already installed:
pip install pandas mlxtend


Step 2: Prepare and Encode the Data
Frequent itemset algorithms in mlxtend expect data in a one-hot encoded boolean DataFrame, where rows represent transactions, columns represent unique items, and values are True or False.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder

# Sample transactional dataset (list of baskets)
transactions = [
    ['Milk', 'Bread', 'Butter'],
    ['Milk', 'Bread', 'Eggs', 'Butter'],
    ['Bread', 'Butter', 'Jam'],
    ['Milk', 'Eggs'],
    ['Milk', 'Bread', 'Butter', 'Coffee'],
    ['Coffee', 'Sugar', 'Milk'],
    ['Bread', 'Jam'],
    ['Milk', 'Bread', 'Eggs', 'Coffee'],
    ['Butter', 'Jam', 'Bread'],
    ['Milk', 'Bread', 'Butter']
]

# Transform transactions into a one-hot encoded boolean DataFrame
te = TransactionEncoder()
te_array = te.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
df = pd.DataFrame(te_array, columns = te.columns_)

print(df.head())

1   True    True   False   True  False   True  False
2   True    True   False  False   True  False  False
3  False   False   False   True  False   True  False
4   True    True    True  False  False   True  False




Step 3: Mine Frequent Itemsets with FP-Growth
Use fpgrowth with a min_support threshold of 0.3 (meaning an itemset must appear in at least 30% of all transactions to be kept).

from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import fpgrowth

# Extract frequent itemsets
frequent_itemsets = fpgrowth(df, min_support = 0.3, use_colnames = True)

# Add a length column for easier filtering and sort by support
frequent_itemsets['length'] = frequent_itemsets['itemsets'].apply(len)
frequent_itemsets = frequent_itemsets.sort_values(by = 'support', ascending = False)

print(frequent_itemsets)

TipChoosing min_support



Setting min_support too high will only return obvious single items (like {Bread} or {Milk}). Setting it too low will flood memory with noisy, coincidental pairs. Start around 0.05 to 0.10 for real-world datasets and adjust based on catalog size.




Step 4: Generate Association Rules
Once frequent itemsets have been identified, they are passed to association_rules() to calculate Confidence, Lift, and other metrics. Here, filter for rules with a Confidence of at least 70% (min_threshold = 0.7).

from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import association_rules

# Generate rules based on confidence
rules = association_rules(
    frequent_itemsets, 
    metric="confidence", 
    min_threshold=0.7
)

# Select and sort the most relevant columns
cols = ['antecedents', 'consequents', 'support', 'confidence', 'lift']
rules_filtered = rules[cols].sort_values(by = 'lift', ascending = False)

print(rules_filtered.to_string(index = False))

Step 5: Interpreting the Output
When reading the final rules_filtered table, look for the intersection of actionable business metrics:

High Lift (\(> 1.2\)): Ensures the items genuinely drive each other’s sales rather than both just being popular items.
Solid Confidence (\(> 0.6\)): Ensures the rule is reliable enough to act upon (e.g., triggering a targeted coupon or checkout recommendation).
Sufficient Support: Guarantees the pattern occurs frequently enough to have a meaningful financial or operational impact.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining
text:
Common Pitfalls to Avoid

The Popular Item Trap: If 80% of customers buy shopping bags, every item will have an 80% confidence rule pointing to {Shopping Bag}. Always verify rules using Lift rather than relying solely on Confidence.
Data Granularity Issues: Mining at the exact SKU level (e.g., Brand X 12oz Whole Milk vs. Brand Y 12oz Whole Milk) often yields support values too low to detect patterns. Aggregate items into meaningful categories (e.g., Dairy - Whole Milk) before running FP-Growth.
Correlation \(\neq\) Causation: A rule {Cereal} -> {Milk} does not necessarily mean promoting cereal will increase milk sales; customers may already be coming to the store intending to buy both.

title: Frequent Itemset Mining
text:
A Note About frozensets
In frequent itemset mining (FIM), algorithms like Apriori and FP-Growth handle thousands or millions of item combinations. The Python frozenset data type plays a crucial role in managing these combinations efficiently.


Unique Dictionary Keys for Support Counting


To track how often itemsets appear in a transactional dataset, algorithms use hash maps (dictionaries) where the itemset is the key and its support count is the value.
Because standard Python set objects are mutable, they are unhashable and cannot be used as dictionary keys.
A frozenset is immutable and hashable, making it a valid and stable key for tracking frequencies (e.g., {frozenset({'Milk', 'Bread'}): 150}).


Order-Independent Item Matching


In retail datasets, the sequence in which items appear in a basket does not matter—buying bread followed by milk is identical to buying milk followed by bread.
frozenset inherently disregards order (frozenset({'Bread', 'Milk'}) is strictly equal to frozenset({'Milk', 'Bread'})), ensuring that identical itemsets bought in different sequences are grouped into the same bucket.


Implementing the Apriori Property (Subset Pruning)


The core of the Apriori algorithm relies on the Downward Closure Property: If an itemset is frequent, all of its subsets must also be frequent.
Frozensets allow algorithms to quickly and mathematically verify subset relationships using built-in set operations (e.g., checking sub_set.issubset(parent_frozenset)).


Library Integration (e.g., mlxtend)


Python libraries designed for association rule mining (such as mlxtend) return mined itemsets wrapped inside frozensets by default. This protects the resulting patterns from accidental in-place modifications while you filter, sort, or generate association rules.

title: Large Language Models
text:
Ollama is an open-source tool designed to let one download, run, and manage powerful open-source LLMs (such as Meta’s Llama 3, Mistral, and Google’s Gemma) locally on one’s own machine (using the machine’s CPU or GPU).






Navigate to the official Ollama website and download the installer for your operating system (macOS, Windows, or Linux).
Open your terminal (or Command Prompt / PowerShell on Windows) and verify that the installation was successful by checking the version:

ollama --version



To run an LLM locally, one needs to download its weights using the pull command; we will use Meta’s llama
ollama pull llama3
Once the download is complete, launch an interactive chat session directly in your terminal:
ollama run llama3

Try asking a data science question: > “Explain the difference between L1 and L2 regularization in simple terms.”
To exit the session: Type /bye or press Ctrl + D.




Check which models are currently stored on the local disk at any time by running:
ollama list
To free up disk space, remove a model using:
ollama rm llama3







Make sure the active virtual environment or notebook kernel has the official Ollama package installed:
pip install ollama



Create a Python script named test_ollama.py or open a Jupyter notebook cell. Use the following code to send a single prompt to your local llama3 instance:

import ollama

# Send a chat request to the locally running model
response = ollama.chat(
    model="llama3",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "Explain the concept of overfitting in machine learning in"
                " exactly two sentences."
            ),
        },
    ],
)

# Extract and print the model's reply
print("Model Response:")
print(response["message"]["content"])

Model Response:
Overfitting in machine learning occurs when a model is too complex and perfectly fits the training data, but performs poorly on new, unseen data because it has memorized the noise and patterns in the training data rather than learning generalizable patterns. This results in a model that is too specialized to the training data and fails to generalize well to new, unseen data, making it less accurate and less useful for making predictions or making decisions.





Guide the model’s persona or output style by prepending a "system" message before the "user" message:

response = ollama.chat(
    model="llama3",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a rigorous data science professor. Keep your answers"
                " concise and academic."
            ),
        },
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is cross-validation?"},
    ],
)

print(response["message"]["content"])

Cross-validation is a statistical technique used to evaluate the performance of a machine learning model by dividing the data into subsets, training and testing the model on each subset in turn, and then combining the results to get an estimate of the model's overall performance.

        (
            "Customer support was incredibly helpful and resolved my issue"

        ),
        (

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print("Original DataFrame:")

    """

title: Large Language Models
text:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Ollama Local RAG)
Build a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system locally using Ollama for querying proprietary or unstructured text corpora without sending private data to external cloud APIs.

Prerequisites

Install the requires Python packages

pip install ollama chromadb

Make sure the Ollama background service is running
Download a text embedding model and a generation model

ollama pull nomic-embed-text
ollama pull llama3


Local RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Pipeline using Ollama and ChromaDB.
This script

ingests custom text documents
generates vector embeddings locally via Ollama (nomic-embed-text)
stores them in an in-memory/local ChromaDB vector database
retrieves the most relevant context for a user query
generates a grounded response using a local LLM (llama3)


import chromadb
import ollama

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration & Constants
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
EMBEDDING_MODEL = "nomic-embed-text"
GENERATION_MODEL = "llama3"
COLLECTION_NAME = "local_rag_docs"


def initialize_vector_database():
  """Initializes ChromaDB client and creates a collection."""
  client = chromadb.Client()
  # Create or get the collection
  collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name=COLLECTION_NAME)
  return collection


def ingest_documents(collection):
  """Ingests sample documents into the vector store by generating local embeddings.

  In a production workflow, you would load these chunks from PDFs, Markdown
  files, or a pandas DataFrame.
  """
  documents = [
      (
          "doc_1",
          "Ollama is an open-source tool that lets users run large language"
          " models locally on their personal hardware, supporting macOS,"
          " Windows, and Linux.",
      ),
      (
          "doc_2",
          "ChromaDB is a lightweight vector database designed to store and query"
          " high-dimensional embeddings efficiently for semantic search and RAG"
          " applications.",
      ),
      (
          "doc_3",
          "Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances LLM responses by"
          " searching a private knowledge base first and injecting the most"
          " relevant text chunks into the prompt context.",
      ),
  ]

  print("[INFO] Generating embeddings and ingesting documents...")
  for doc_id, text in documents:
    # 1. Generate local embedding using Ollama
    response = ollama.embeddings(model=EMBEDDING_MODEL, prompt=text)
    embedding = response["embedding"]

    # 2. Add document, embedding, and metadata to ChromaDB
    collection.add(
        ids=[doc_id], embeddings=[embedding], documents=[text]
    )
  print(f"[INFO] Successfully ingested {len(documents)} documents.")


def query_rag_system(collection, user_query):
  """Retrieves relevant context based on semantic similarity and prompts the local LLM."""
  print(f"\n[QUERY] User Question: '{user_query}'")

  # 1. Generate embedding for the user query
  query_response = ollama.embeddings(model=EMBEDDING_MODEL, prompt=user_query)
  query_embedding = query_response["embedding"]

  # 2. Query ChromaDB for the top K most similar text chunks
  results = collection.query(query_embeddings=[query_embedding], n_results=2)
  retrieved_docs = results["documents"][0]

  # 3. Construct context block from retrieved chunks
  context = "\n\n".join(retrieved_docs)
  print(f"[INFO] Retrieved Context Chunks:\n{context}\n")

  # 4. Construct prompt combining context and user query
  system_prompt = (
      "You are a helpful assistant. Answer the user's question accurately"
      " using ONLY the provided context below. If you do not know the answer"
      " based on the context, state that you cannot find it."
  )

  user_prompt = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {user_query}"

  # 5. Call local LLM via Ollama chat endpoint
  print("[INFO] Generating response from local model...")
  response = ollama.chat(
      model=GENERATION_MODEL,
      messages=[
          {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
          {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt},
      ],
  )

  return response["message"]["content"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
  # Step 1: Set up vector database
  vector_collection = initialize_vector_database()

  # Step 2: Ingest knowledge base documents
  ingest_documents(vector_collection)

  # Step 3: Run a sample query against our local RAG pipeline
  question = "How does RAG improve large language model responses?"
  answer = query_rag_system(vector_collection, question)

  print("=== Final LLM Answer ===")
  print(answer)

title: EDA
text:
What is Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)?
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the critical bridge between raw data collection and advanced machine learning modeling. Before training algorithms, building complex pipelines, or deploying neural networks, one must first understand the structural landscape of the data.
Think of EDA as an investigative process. Instead of jumping straight into assumptions or predictive models, one acts like a detective — using visualization, statistical summary metrics, and data transformation tools to interrogate the dataset, uncover hidden anomalies, check assumptions, and surface core patterns.



The Core Objectives of EDA

Understand Data Structure & Integrity: Know the data shapes, column types, missing values, and duplicate rows.
Uncover Distribution Patterns: Identify whether features are normally distributed, heavily skewed, or prone to extreme outliers.
Detect Relationships & Correlations: Spot multi-collinearity or linear/non-linear relationships between predictors and target variables.
Guide Feature Engineering: Inform decisions on scaling, normalization, imputation strategies, and categorical encoding.




Step-by-Step EDA Workflow
A robust EDA workflow typically flows through four distinct phases:

1. Data Inspection & Cleaning

Dimensions Check:

Inspect the dataset’s row and column counts using df.shape.

Data Types Audit:

Verify that numerical columns are stored as floats/integers and categorical features are mapped correctly.

Missing Value Analysis:

Quantify missingness using .isnull().sum() and visualize missing data patterns to decide between imputation or dropping rows/columns.

Duplicate Removal:

Check for and drop redundant duplicate records.




2. Univariate Analysis (Examining One Variable at a Time)

Numerical Features:

Calculate central tendencies (mean, median) and dispersion (standard deviation, interquartile range).

Visualize distributions using histograms, kernel density estimation (KDE) plots, or boxplots to spot skewed data distributions and outliers.

Categorical Features:

Calculate frequency counts and proportions using .value_counts().
Visualize cardinalities and class imbalances using countplots or bar charts.




3. Bivariate & Multivariate Analysis (Exploring Relationships)

Numerical vs. Numerical:

Use scatterplots or pairplots (sns.pairplot) to inspect joint distributions and correlations.
Compute a correlation matrix (Pearson or Spearman) and visualize it via a heatmap to detect multi-collinearity.

Categorical vs. Numerical:

Compare distributions across groups using boxplots, violin plots, or faceted histograms (sns.FacetGrid).

Categorical vs. Categorical:

Utilize grouped bar charts or contingency tables (cross-tabs) to evaluate associations.




4. Hypothesis Generation & Insight Synthesis

Document initial findings, surprising correlations, and data anomalies.
Formulate concrete hypotheses to test during feature engineering and model building (e.g., “Customer churn spikes significantly when tenure is under 6 months combined with high support ticket frequency”).





Best Practices

Never Skip Visualizations: Summary statistics can lie (consider Anscombe’s Quartet, where datasets with identical means and correlations look completely different when plotted). Always back up numbers with plots.
Beware of Data Leakage: Perform EDA primarily on the training set. Keep the test set locked away to prevent inadvertent bias from bleeding into exploratory insights.
Document: Keep a clean, well-commented notebook where every visual output is accompanied by a brief interpretive takeaway sentence.

title: Classification
text:
In machine learning, classification is a core type of supervised learning where the goal is to predict the categorical label (class) of a given observation based on its input features.
Unlike regression — which predicts continuous numerical values (such as predicting a house price or temperature) — classification assigns data points into discrete, predefined buckets or categories.

title: Classification
text:
Logistic Regression


Probabilistic Output: Unlike the Perceptron, Logistic Regression uses the sigmoid function to map raw linear outputs to values between 0 and 1. Access predicted probabilities using predict_proba().
Regularization: scikit-learn applies \(L_2\) regularization by default (C=1.0), which penalizes large coefficient weights to prevent overfitting.
Feature Scaling: Standardizing features with StandardScaler remains important so that regularization applies uniformly across all features and solver algorithms (like lbfgs) converge efficiently.

title: Text Summarization with Hugging Face
text:
Text Summarization
Text summarization is the process of distilling a long piece of text into a shorter version while preserving its most critical information, meaning, and core context.
The Hugging Face library (transformers) serves as the industry standard for implementing state-of-the-art summarization pipelines with just a few lines of code.


The Two Main Paradigms of Summarization
Before writing code, it is essential to understand the two primary ways models summarize text:

Extractive Summarization:


How it works: Extracts the most important sentences or phrases directly from the original text and concatenates them to form a summary.
Analogy: Using a yellow highlighter to mark key sentences in a textbook chapter.


Abstractive Summarization:


How it works: Generates new sentences by “reading” the text, understanding its semantic meaning, and rephrasing it in its own words (similar to how humans summarize).
Analogy: Reading an article and writing a fresh, concise paragraph in your own voice. Hugging Face pipelines predominantly excel here using transformer architectures.




Key Parameters to Tune
When working with summarization pipelines, adjust these generation parameters:

max_length / min_length: Controls how long or short the output summary can be.
num_beams: Controls beam search. Higher values (e.g., 4 or 5) explore more potential word combinations for a better summary, at the cost of slower inference speed.
do_sample: If set to True, the model uses probabilistic sampling (controlled by temperature or top_k/top_p), which can introduce creativity or variation into the summaries.



Example

import os
import pymupdf
from transformers import pipeline
import textwrap
import requests

def extract_text_from_pdf(pdf_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Opens a PDF file and extracts all text content page by page.
    """
    if not os.path.exists(pdf_path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The file {pdf_path} was not found.")
    
    text = ""
    with pymupdf.open(pdf_path) as doc:
        for page in doc:
            page_text = page.get_text()
            if page_text:
                text += page_text + "\n"
                
    return text.strip()

def summarize_text(text: str, max_sentences: int = 10) -> str:
    """
    Uses the modern Hugging Face 'text-generation' pipeline with an instruction-tuned model
    to generate a concise summary constrained to a maximum number of sentences.
    """
    if not text:
        return "No text could be extracted from the PDF."

    print("Loading local text-generation pipeline...")
    # Use a standard open-source instruction model supported by text-generation
    summarizer = pipeline("text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct")
    
    # Construct a clear prompt enforcing the sentence limit constraint
    prompt = f"""
    Please provide a concise summary of the following text. 
    Your summary must be strictly no more than {max_sentences} sentences long.

    Text:
    {text[:4000]}  # Truncate to fit model context window if necessary
    """
    
    print("Generating summary...")
    # Format as a chat message for instruction-tuned models
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant that summarizes documents accurately."},
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
    
    output = summarizer(messages, max_new_tokens=300, do_sample=False)
    
    # Extract the generated response text from the chat output structure
    summary_text = output[0]['generated_text'][-1]['content']
    
    # Post-processing: Ensure sentence count is strictly <= max_sentences
    sentences = [s.strip() for s in summary_text.split('.') if s.strip()]
    if len(sentences) > max_sentences:
        sentences = sentences[:max_sentences]
        summary_text = '. '.join(sentences) + '.'
        
    return summary_text

title: Natural Language Processing
text:
Core Tasks

Text Classification: Categorizing text into predefined labels (e.g., spam detection, sentiment analysis of product reviews).
Named Entity Recognition (NER): Extracting key entities from text, such as names, dates, organizations, or medical terms.
Machine Translation: Automatically translating text or speech from one language to another (e.g., Google Translate).
Text Summarization: Condensing long documents or articles into short, cohesive summaries.
Question Answering & Conversational AI: Building systems (like chatbots or virtual assistants) that can parse a query and retrieve or generate precise answers.

title: Natural Language Processing
section: The Evolution: From Linguistics to Transformers
text:
The Evolution: From Linguistics to Transformers

Traditional NLP (Rule-Based & Statistical): Early systems relied on heavy human intervention, grammar rules, regular expressions, and statistical models like TF-IDF and Naive Bayes.
Deep Learning Era: The introduction of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and LSTMs allowed models to process sequences of words and capture short-term context.
The Transformer Revolution: Modern NLP is dominated by Transformer architectures (like BERT, GPT, and T5) powered by self-attention mechanisms. These models process entire sentences in parallel, capturing deep, nuanced context across massive datasets.

Text Classification

The Text Classification Workflow
A text classification pipeline involves five sequential steps:

Data Collection & Preparation: Gathering the text dataset and ensuring the target labels are clean and well-defined.
Train-Test Splitting: Partitioning the data to prevent data leakage and evaluate the model objectively on unseen data.
Text Feature Extraction (Vectorization): Machine learning algorithms require numerical inputs, not raw strings. One must convert text into numerical vectors using techniques like TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) or Bag-of-Words.
Model Training: Fitting a classification algorithm (such as Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, or Support Vector Machines) to the training features.

Best Practices

Leverage Pipelines: Always wrap the text vectorizer and model inside a sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline. This prevents data leakage (where test statistics accidentally influence training vectorization) and simplifies deployment.
Handle Imbalanced Data: If one class heavily dominates your dataset (e.g., 98% non-fraudulent transactions), rely on F1-Score, Precision, and Recall rather than raw accuracy.
Experiment with N-grams: Including unigrams (single words) alongside bigrams (ngram_range = (1, 2)) helps capture short contextual phrases like “not good” instead of just treating words independently.





Named entity Recognition
Named Entity Recognition is a subtask of Information Extraction that seeks to locate and classify named entities mentioned in text into predefined categories, such as Persons, Organizations, Locations, Dates, Monetary Values, and more.


The Named Entity Recognition Workflow
Building and applying an NER pipeline involves four primary stages:

Text Preprocessing & Tokenization: Cleaning the raw text and splitting it into individual words or tokens while preserving sentence boundaries.
Feature Engineering / Representation: Transforming tokens into numerical or vector representations (such as word embeddings or part-of-speech tags) for traditional machine learning, or feeding raw sequences directly into deep learning architectures.
Model Training & Sequence Labeling: Using sequence labeling algorithms — such as Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), BiLSTM-CRFs, or state-of-the-art Transformer models (like BERT/RoBERTa via Hugging Face) — to predict entity tags (often encoded using schemes like IOB: Inside, Outside, Beginning).
Post-Processing & Evaluation: Extracting the recognized entity spans, mapping them to their canonical types, and evaluating performance using entity-level Precision, Recall, and F1-Score.



NER with spaCy
In modern data science, one rarely trains an NER model from scratch unless one has specialized domain corpora (like medical records or legal contracts). Instead, one uses robust pre-trained libraries like spaCy or Hugging Face Transformers.
A clean, reproducible script using spaCy to perform off-the-shelf Named Entity Recognition:

Best Practices

Understand IOB Tagging Schemes: Most sequence labelers use B- (Beginning), I- (Inside), and O (Outside). For instance, “San Francisco” would be tagged as B-LOC followed by I-LOC. Ensuring correct scheme handling is vital when building custom models.
Leverage Transfer Learning: For domain-specific tasks (e.g., extracting legal clauses or biomedical genes), fine-tuning a pre-trained transformer model using frameworks like Hugging Face transformers yields vastly superior results compared to rule-based or traditional machine learning approaches.
Entity Disambiguation & Linking: Recognizing an entity is just step one. Real-world systems often require Entity Linking to tie a mention (like “Apple”) to a unique knowledge base ID (such as Wikidata Q312) to resolve ambiguity.





Text Summarization
Text summarization is the process of distilling a long piece of text into a shorter version while preserving its most critical information, meaning, and core context.
The Hugging Face library (transformers) serves as the industry standard for implementing state-of-the-art summarization pipelines with just a few lines of code.


The Two Main Paradigms of Summarization
Before writing code, it is essential to understand the two primary ways models summarize text:

Extractive Summarization:


How it works: Extracts the most important sentences or phrases directly from the original text and concatenates them to form a summary.
Analogy: Using a yellow highlighter to mark key sentences in a textbook chapter.


Abstractive Summarization:


How it works: Generates new sentences by “reading” the text, understanding its semantic meaning, and rephrasing it in its own words (similar to how humans summarize).
Analogy: Reading an article and writing a fresh, concise paragraph in your own voice. Hugging Face pipelines predominantly excel here using transformer architectures.




Key Parameters to Tune
When working with summarization pipelines, adjust these generation parameters:

max_length / min_length: Controls how long or short the output summary can be.
num_beams: Controls beam search. Higher values (e.g., 4 or 5) explore more potential word combinations for a better summary, at the cost of slower inference speed.
do_sample: If set to True, the model uses probabilistic sampling (controlled by temperature or top_k/top_p), which can introduce creativity or variation into the summaries.

def extract_text_from_pdf(pdf_path: str) -> str:
    """
    Opens a PDF file and extracts all text content page by page.
    """
    if not os.path.exists(pdf_path):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The file {pdf_path} was not found.")
    
    text = ""
    with pymupdf.open(pdf_path) as doc:
        for page in doc:
            page_text = page.get_text()
            if page_text:
                text += page_text + "\n"
                
    return text.strip()

def summarize_text(text: str, max_sentences: int = 10) -> str:
    """
    Uses the modern Hugging Face 'text-generation' pipeline with an instruction-tuned model
    to generate a concise summary constrained to a maximum number of sentences.
    """
    if not text:
        return "No text could be extracted from the PDF."

    print("Loading local text-generation pipeline...")
    # Use a standard open-source instruction model supported by text-generation
    summarizer = pipeline("text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct")
    
    # Construct a clear prompt enforcing the sentence limit constraint
    prompt = f"""
    Please provide a concise summary of the following text. 
    Your summary must be strictly no more than {max_sentences} sentences long.

    Text:
    {text[:4000]}  # Truncate to fit model context window if necessary
    """
    
    print("Generating summary...")
    # Format as a chat message for instruction-tuned models
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant that summarizes documents accurately."},
        {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
    ]
    
    output = summarizer(messages, max_new_tokens=300, do_sample=False)
    
    # Extract the generated response text from the chat output structure
    summary_text = output[0]['generated_text'][-1]['content']
    
    # Post-processing: Ensure sentence count is strictly <= max_sentences
    sentences = [s.strip() for s in summary_text.split('.') if s.strip()]
    if len(sentences) > max_sentences:
        sentences = sentences[:max_sentences]
        summary_text = '. '.join(sentences) + '.'
        
    return summary_text

title: Deep Learning
text:
If machine learning is about teaching computers to learn from data using statistical algorithms, deep learning is about mimicking the human brain to solve complex, high-dimensional problems like computer vision, speech recognition, and generative AI.

Deep Learning is a specialized subset of Machine Learning (ML) based on artificial neural networks with multiple layers (hence “deep”).
While traditional machine learning models often require manual feature engineering (e.g., one has to tell the model what attributes of a house or an image matter), deep learning models automatically discover the representations and features needed for detection or prediction directly from raw data.


The Anatomy of a Neural Network
The building blocks of deep learning:

Neurons (Nodes): The basic units of computation. They take input data, multiply it by weights, add a bias, and pass the result through an activation function (like ReLU or Sigmoid) to introduce non-linearity.
Layers:

Input Layer: Receives the raw data (pixels, text tokens, tabular numbers).
Hidden Layers: The “deep” part of the network. These intermediate layers extract increasingly abstract features (e.g., in an image model, early layers might detect edges, middle layers detect shapes, and deep layers recognize faces).
Output Layer: Produces the final prediction or classification.

Backpropagation & Optimization: The learning mechanism. The model calculates its error (using a loss function) and uses gradient descent to update the network’s weights backwards, minimizing the error over time.




Major Deep Learning Architectures
Different types of data require different neural network architectures :

Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs / MLPs): The simplest architecture where data moves in one direction. Great for structured/tabular data.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs): Designed specifically for grid-like data such as images and video. They use convolutional filters to capture spatial hierarchies.
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) & LSTMs: Built for sequential data like time-series or text, though largely superseded by transformers.
Transformers: The architecture powering modern Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), relying heavily on self-attention mechanisms to process sequences in parallel.

import torch

# Define the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)
class SonarNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim):
        super(SonarNN, self).__init__()
        self.layer1 = nn.Linear(input_dim, 32)
        self.relu1 = nn.ReLU()
        self.layer2 = nn.Linear(32, 16)
        self.relu2 = nn.ReLU()
        self.output = nn.Linear(16, 1)
        self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid()
        
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.relu1(self.layer1(x))
        x = self.relu2(self.layer2(x))
        x = self.sigmoid(self.output(x))
        return x
